summary: I developed an interactive web application that analyzes historical space landing sites, evaluating their power generation efficiency and the stability of their communication links with Earth. Users can also select custom landing coordinates and directly compare their performance metrics against past missions. This addresses the challenge by turning complex orbital and environmental data into an accessible visual tool. It is important because optimizing energy and communication is critical for mission survival, helping planners and enthusiasts identify the safest locations for future exploration.
details:
ı built a 3D web tool that helps find the best spots to place solar panels on the Moon’s far side and South Pole while tracking Earth visibility for communications. It combines real NASA elevation and surface imagery with JPL Horizons ephemeris data to generate local terrain around candidate landing sites. From there, it calculates sunlight exposure, shadowing from surrounding craters, vacuum thermal effects, and solar cell efficiency over time.
Instead of relying on flat assumptions or broad orbital maps, this gives mission planners a fast way to evaluate both power generation and communication blackouts in one place. The goal is to help future lunar missions avoid shadowed or thermally harsh zones before landing.
I built the interactive 3D interface with TypeScript, Three.js, and Vite, and wrote the visibility and ephemeris backend in Python using NumPy and FastAPI. Bringing live physics calculations and real lunar data together inside a browser was the most creative part of the project. While designing it, I had to account for horizon obstructions, lunar curvature, regolith heating, dust, and local terrain slopes.
